items.title: Open-Air Cinema at La Villette
items.area: Parc de la Villette · Prairie du Triangle
items.transit: M5 to Porte de Pantin — or walk the canal from home in ~40 min
items.why: The 35th edition, and it ends this Sunday. This year's theme is the forest. Bring a bottle and a blanket, get there by 20:15 for the 21:00 film. The canal walk up from Jaurès at dusk is half the pleasure — it is genuinely one of the best free nights in Paris and it is basically in your neighbourhood.

items.title: Paris Plages
items.area: Bassin de la Villette + Seine banks
items.transit: M5 to Stalingrad, or a 20-min walk straight up the canal
items.why: 24th edition. The Bassin de la Villette stretch is the one locals actually use — pétanque, deckchairs, open-air dancing, cheap drinks — and it is the closest big summer thing to your flat. Skip the Seine section, it is mostly tourists. Go on a weekday evening around 19:00 when the light is good and the crowds have thinned.

items.title: The Olympic Cauldron Rises at Sunset
items.times: Rises at sunset, stays up until 02:00 · visible on the ground from 10:00
items.transit: M8 to Concorde, or M1 to Tuileries
items.why: The balloon-and-flame cauldron from the 2024 Games comes back every summer and floats over the Tuileries after dark. It is free, it is genuinely beautiful, and almost nobody plans for it. Pair it with a walk along the Seine — sunset in mid-August is around 21:00, so aim to be there by 20:45.

nearby.text: Pont des Arts + Seine walk → 10 min
Fête des Tuileries funfair → on site

items.title: Paris Jazz Festival — Parc Floral
items.transit: M1 to Château de Vincennes, then ~10 min walk
items.why: Concerts by serious French and international jazz musicians for the price of a coffee — €2.70 gets you into the park and the music is free. Bring a picnic and lie on the grass. This is the single best value cultural thing running in Paris right now, and it runs every weekend until early September.

nearby.text: Parc Floral butterfly garden → on site

items.title: Classique au Vert — Open-Air Classical
items.transit: M1 to Château de Vincennes, then ~10 min walk
items.why: The classical sibling of the jazz festival, on the same lawn, same €2.70. Chamber ensembles and small orchestras playing outdoors in August. If you have never done a concert lying on grass with a bottle of wine, do this one before September 4.

items.title: Free Stargazing Evenings in Paris Parks
items.transit: Varies — Jardin d'Éole and Buttes-Chaumont are your closest sites
items.why: The Association Française d'Astronomie sets up telescopes in Paris parks on summer nights and lets anyone look through them, for free. Jardin d'Éole is a 15-minute walk from you. Check their calendar for which park is hosting on a given night — it rotates, so this needs one click before you go.

items.title: Salsa & Swing on the Péniche Marcounet
items.area: Quai des Célestins, near Pont Marie
items.transit: M7 to Pont Marie, or a 35-min walk down the canal and along the Seine
items.why: A barge moored on the Seine that turns into an open-air dance floor at weekends. Nobody minds if you cannot dance — half the crowd is learning. Free, unpretentious, and about as romantic as a Sunday afternoon in Paris gets. Sunday swing is the better of the two.

items.title: Fête des Tuileries Funfair
items.transit: M8 to Concorde
items.why: A proper old-fashioned funfair in the Tuileries with a big wheel that gives you one of the best cheap views in Paris. Worth combining with the Olympic cauldron after dark — they are in the same garden. Ten days left.

items.title: La Javelle Summer Guinguette
items.transit: M5 direct to Bercy
items.why: Riverside guinguette with DJs, live music, karaoke and comedy nights, free to get in. It is a single Metro line from you with no changes. Good low-effort answer to 'we want to be outside with a drink and something happening'.

items.title: Leandro Erlich — Grand Palais
items.transit: M1 to Champs-Élysées–Clemenceau
items.why: The biggest Erlich show ever staged in Europe. He is the artist who builds swimming pools you can walk under and buildings you can climb sideways — optical-illusion installations you physically enter. It is the rare major exhibition that is genuinely fun rather than dutiful, and it is very good on a rainy or blisteringly hot day.

items.title: Hilma af Klint — Grand Palais
items.transit: M1 to Champs-Élysées–Clemenceau
items.why: Her first showing in France, and it closes August 30. Af Klint was painting large abstract canvases years before Kandinsky and then asked for them to stay hidden for 20 years after her death. Seeing them in person is a genuinely strange experience. Closing soon — this is a now-or-never one.

items.title: Beyond the Streets — Graffiti & Street Art
items.transit: M5 to Porte de Pantin
items.why: 3,600 m² and over 100 major graffiti and street artists, in the huge iron hall at La Villette. It is a short hop from you on line 5. Best move: do the exhibition in the afternoon, then stay in the park for the open-air cinema at 21:00 — same site, one trip, whole day sorted.

items.title: Two Photography Retrospectives — Jeu de Paume
items.area: Jeu de Paume, Jardin des Tuileries
items.transit: M8 to Concorde
items.why: Jeu de Paume is the serious photography house in Paris and it is small enough to do properly in 90 minutes without museum fatigue. Two retrospectives running at once until late September. Then walk out into the Tuileries and stay for the cauldron at sunset.
items.imageSubject: Galerie nationale du Jeu de Paume

items.title: Gianni Versace Retrospective — Musée Maillol
items.transit: M8 to Invalides / M12 to Rue du Bac
items.why: A full Versace retrospective in a small, manageable museum — the archive pieces are extraordinary up close, and Maillol never gets the crush that the big houses do. Runs until the end of October, so this is one to keep in your back pocket for a grey autumn Sunday rather than a sunny August one.

items.title: 1913–1923: L'esprit du temps — Quai Branly
items.area: Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac
items.transit: M9 to Alma–Marceau, then walk
items.why: The decade that broke and remade European culture, told through the objects that arrived in Paris from elsewhere during it. Quai Branly is also one of the best buildings in Paris — the Jean Nouvel green wall and the garden are worth the trip on their own, and the garden is free.

items.title: Nocturnes d'Été — Palais de Tokyo
items.times: One evening per week — check the site for this week's date
items.transit: M9 to Iéna
items.why: Palais de Tokyo is open until midnight most nights anyway, but during the summer nocturnes the contemporary art shows are free. It is the least reverent museum in Paris — concrete, loud, occasionally baffling — and much better as a date than a worthy afternoon at the Louvre. Confirm the evening on their site before you go.

items.title: Open-Air Theatre — Jardin Shakespeare
items.priceNote: Free to €25 depending on the show
items.transit: M1 to Les Sablons, then a walk through the Bois
items.why: A green amphitheatre hidden inside the Bois de Boulogne, planted with every species Shakespeare mentions, staging open-air theatre all summer. Very few Parisians have been. It is far, so treat it as a whole afternoon: walk in the Bois, then the show.

items.title: Rock en Seine
items.transit: M9 to Pont de Sèvres + shuttle, or M10 to Boulogne
items.why: The big one at the end of August, in the grounds of a former royal estate. The Cure close it on the 30th, Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds play the 28th, Tyler the Creator opens on the 26th, Lorde headlines the 27th. Day tickets beat passes unless you want all five. Book now if you want it — this sells through.

items.title: Journées Européennes du Patrimoine
items.priceNote: Free — but the good sites need booking
items.transit: Everywhere — pick sites near home first
items.why: The single best weekend of the Paris year and it is worth planning for now. Thousands of buildings normally shut to the public open their doors for free: ministries, private hôtels particuliers, the Élysée, Freemason lodges, working ateliers. The 2026 theme is architectural heritage in danger. The catch is that the desirable sites open bookings in late August and are gone within hours — set a reminder for the last week of August.

items.title: Esports World Cup
items.transit: M12 to Porte de Versailles
items.why: Included because it is genuinely unlike anything else on this list: a 500 m² gaming floor, showmatches, talks and live music inside the Expo halls. Worth it if you are at all curious about what a 20,000-person crowd watching a video game feels like. Skip it otherwise.

items.title: Jazz à la Villette
items.area: Parc de la Villette · Philharmonie, Trabendo, Grande Halle
items.transit: M5 to Porte de Pantin — twenty minutes, no changes
items.why: The best thing in this whole guide for the next fortnight, and it happens to be twenty minutes up line 5. Ten days of jazz, soul, funk and hip-hop across the Villette venues. This year: Snarky Puppy with the Metropole Orkest, GoGo Penguin, Selah Sue, Cymande, Kokoroko, Emma-Jean Thackray, and Roberto Fonseca with Vincent Segal. Book now — the Philharmonie nights go first, and the cheap upper tiers there are genuinely good seats.
items.source: La Villette / Jazz à la Villette

items.title: Techno Parade
items.transit: Walk to the route — it usually passes close to République
items.why: A dozen sound systems on lorries and several hundred thousand people dancing through the middle of Paris on a Saturday afternoon, for free. It is not subtle and it is not for everyone, but it is one of the few days the city gives its streets over completely. The route generally comes near République, so you can join for an hour and walk home. Note it clashes with the heritage weekend.

items.title: Lauryn Hill — Accor Arena
items.transit: M5 direct to Bercy — no changes from home
items.why: Ms Lauryn Hill at Bercy, with YG Marley and Zion Marley supporting. She tours rarely and cancels sometimes, so this is a real one. Line 5 goes straight there from your street, which makes the trip home after an arena show far less grim than usual.

items.title: Ayo — La Cigale
items.transit: M2 to Pigalle or Anvers
items.why: Soul and folk in the loveliest mid-size hall in Paris — La Cigale is an 1887 theatre with a balcony, and it is small enough that the balcony is worth having. Twenty minutes from home and the sort of evening where you can walk down through Pigalle for a drink afterwards.

items.title: Yemi Alade — La Cigale
items.transit: M2 to Pigalle or Anvers
items.why: One of the biggest Afrobeats voices in the world, in a room that holds barely a thousand. Nobody sits down. If you want a night that is pure dancing without going to a club at midnight, this is it.

items.title: European Aquatics Championships
items.area: Seine at Bras de Grenelle · high diving at Port Debilly · Saint-Denis
items.priceNote: Open water and high diving free from the riverbank · pool sessions ticketed
items.transit: M6 to Bir-Hakeim for the river events
items.why: This finishes tomorrow and it is free to watch the best bits. The open-water swimming happens in the Seine between Bir-Hakeim and the Île aux Cygnes, and the high diving — people falling twenty-seven metres off a platform into the river — is free from the bank at Port Debilly. If you do one thing this weekend, this is the one that will not come round again.

items.title: Qatar Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe
items.times: Two days, the main race Sunday afternoon
items.transit: M1 to Porte Maillot, then the free racecourse shuttle
items.why: The biggest flat race in Europe, on the first weekend of October, in a park at the edge of the Bois de Boulogne. It is a proper day out: hats, picnics, sixty thousand people, and about two minutes of actual racing that everyone loses their mind over. Buy general admission in advance, take a picnic, and do not bother with the expensive stands.

items.title: 20 km de Paris
items.area: Start and finish at the Eiffel Tower
items.transit: M6 to Bir-Hakeim
items.why: The 48th edition, and the best mass-participation race in the city: it starts on the Pont d’Iéna under the Eiffel Tower, runs past the Trocadéro and the Arc de Triomphe, loops through the Bois de Boulogne and Roland-Garros, and finishes back at the tower. Twenty kilometres is a real but reachable target from a standing start in mid-August — eight weeks is enough if you start now. Entries close when it fills.

items.title: Rolex Paris Masters
items.times: Nine days, day and night sessions
items.transit: RER A to Nanterre-Préfecture
items.why: The last Masters 1000 of the season, and its 40th edition — effectively every top-ten player in one indoor arena before the season ends. The trick is the first three days: cheap tickets, and a ground pass gets you several matches on the same day instead of one. The finals weekend costs four times as much for less tennis.

items.title: Fête de Ganesh
items.area: Temple Sri Manicka Vinayakar Alayam, 17 rue Pajol
items.transit: M12 to Marx Dormoy, or a 20-minute walk
items.why: The Tamil community of Paris has processed Ganesh through the streets of La Chapelle every year since 1995, and it is fifteen minutes from your door. Nageshvaram players and drummers lead, then dancers carrying kavadi arches of peacock feathers and pots of burning camphor, then Ganesh himself on a decorated float with his brother Muruga behind. Twenty-five thousand people, coconuts smashed on the road, free food afterwards. Arrive by 10:00 for the procession leaving the temple.
